questions.statement: Which sentence correctly begins a narrative with an action?
questions.context: A student is asked to write a short narrative.

options.text: Ana pushed the gate open and ran the last hundred metres to the bus.
options.feedback: Correct. The sentence begins with a verb and moves the character forward, which is what opens a narrative.

options.text: Ana pushed the gate open, and then Ana ran, and then Ana arrived.
options.feedback: Wrong. The sentence repeats 'Ana' three times, which destroys any sense of movement.

options.text: A girl ran, and she ran, and the bus was there.
options.feedback: Wrong. The sentence repeats 'ran' with no new information and stalls the action.

options.text: Ana is a girl who runs to the bus every morning.
options.feedback: Wrong. The sentence is a description of a habitual routine, not an unfolding event.

questions.explanation:
A narrative opens with an action in the past simple, using sentence structure to move the reader forward.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that maintains correct tense throughout the narrative.
questions.context: A student is asked to write a short narrative about a journey.

options.text: The bus was late, so the driver waits while the passengers find their seats.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Waits' and 'find' shift to the present and break the past frame of the narrative.

options.text: The bus was late, so the driver waited while the passengers found their seats.
options.feedback: Correct. All clauses use the past simple, which is the consistent tense for a sequence of completed events.

options.text: The bus was late, so the driver waited while the passengers are finding their seats.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Are finding' shifts the final clause to the present continuous mid-narrative.

options.text: The bus is late, so the driver was waiting while the passengers found their seats.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is late' is present and inconsistent with the past simple around it.

questions.explanation:
A short past narrative keeps its tenses consistent, since a shift to the present pulls the reader out of the sequence.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that best creates tension at the point where the character loses the keys.
questions.context: A student is building tension in a narrative.

options.text: Patricio put his hand in his pocket and found something to take with him.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Something' is vague and communicates no sense of loss or discovery.

options.text: Patricio put his hand in his pocket and found his keys.
options.feedback: Wrong. Naming the keys removes the problem entirely and dissolves the tension.

options.text: Patricio put his hand in his pocket and found nothing but an old bus ticket.
options.feedback: Correct. Naming the bus ticket precisely shows what was there and leaves the reader to share the character's alarm.

options.text: Patricio put his hand in his pocket and found one thing that was not what he wanted.
options.feedback: Wrong. The sentence is hedged and does not identify what was found.

questions.explanation:
Tension comes from a specific detail that the reader recognises as wrong, not from stating the problem outright.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly orders events using a time connector.
questions.context: A student is setting the sequence of a narrative.

options.text: After the storm passed they walked the length of the flooded street to see damage.
options.feedback: Wrong. The sentence lacks the comma that normally follows 'after' plus a clause, and it ends abruptly.

options.text: After they walked the length of the flooded street, the storm passed to see the damage.
options.feedback: Wrong. The connector is attached to the wrong clause, so the order of events is reversed.

options.text: After the storm passes, they walk the length of the flooded street to see the damage.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Passes' and 'walk' are present tense, so the sequence is not anchored in the past.

options.text: After the storm passed, they walked the length of the flooded street to see the damage.
options.feedback: Correct. 'After' introduces the earlier event and the main clause carries the later one, in a consistent past tense.

questions.explanation:
Connectors such as after, before and when require the earlier event in the subordinate clause and the later one in the main clause.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that reports speech correctly without altering the speaker's words.
questions.context: A student is writing dialogue inside a narrative.

options.text: The teacher said that the results would be published on Friday.
options.feedback: Correct. Quotation marks preserve the speaker's exact words and the present tense is natural within direct speech.

options.text: The teacher told that the results would be published on Friday.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Told' requires an indirect object, as in told us, and cannot stand alone here.

options.text: The teacher announced, 'The results will be published on Friday.'
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Said that' backshifts and adds a complementiser, so the original wording is not preserved exactly.

options.text: The teacher said the results would be published on Friday.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Said that' backshifts the tense, which changes the wording the reader hears.

questions.explanation:
Direct speech with quotation marks preserves the original words, while reported speech changes the tense and sometimes the pronouns.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the ending that most effectively closes the story of a delayed bus.
questions.context: A student is ending a narrative.

options.text: The bus eventually arrived, which was the end of the story for the bus.
options.feedback: Wrong. The phrase 'the end of the story for the bus' is an intrusive comment on the narration itself.

options.text: The bus arrived at last, and Patricio was the only one still waiting.
options.feedback: Correct. The final detail leaves one character behind the others, which gives the ending a lingering effect.

options.text: The end of the story is that the bus came at last.
options.feedback: Wrong. The sentence names the ending rather than presenting the final moment of the action.

options.text: The bus arrived at last, and it was late, and everyone was annoyed.
options.feedback: Wrong. The ending repeats 'bus' and 'late' and states the obvious without adding anything.

questions.explanation:
An effective ending presents the last action concretely; a weak one comments on or announces the ending.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sequence keeps the cause before its effect?
questions.context: A student is checking the logical order of a narrative.

options.text: The lifts stopped, the power failed, and the staff on the tenth floor began to walk down.
options.feedback: Wrong. The lifts cannot stop before the power that supplies them has failed.

options.text: The staff on the tenth floor began to walk down, the lifts stopped, and the power failed.
options.feedback: Wrong. The sequence runs backwards, since the response appears before the events that produced it.

options.text: The power failed, the lifts stopped, and the staff on the tenth floor began to walk down.
options.feedback: Correct. The power failure causes the lifts to stop, which in turn leaves the staff walking, so the chain runs in order.

options.text: The staff walked down, the power failed, and then the lifts stopped.
options.feedback: Wrong. The staff walk before the failure that would explain their walking.

questions.explanation:
Narrative sequences normally follow cause and effect, so reversing the chain makes the events appear unmotivated.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which revision adds narrative momentum to the sentence?
questions.context: A student is improving a narrative paragraph.

options.text: He runs, he stumbles, he catches the rail, and he keeps going.
options.feedback: Wrong. Present tense changes the time frame, and the repeated pronouns read mechanically.

options.text: He was running and he was stumbling and he caught the rail and he kept going.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was running' and 'was stumbling' form a continuous chain that leaves no sense of completed action.

options.text: He ran and then he stumbled and then he caught the rail and then he kept going.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'And then' repeated five times slows the sentence down and defeats the purpose.

options.text: He ran, stumbled, caught the rail and kept going without stopping.
options.feedback: Correct. The verbs in sequence carry the action forward without pausing, which creates momentum.

questions.explanation:
Momentum in a narrative comes from chaining actions in the past simple with minimal connective tissue.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The child saw the storm arrive and counted the seconds between the thunder and the rain. Which point of view is used?
questions.context: A student is checking the point of view in a narrative.

options.text: First person or third person focused on the child, because only what the child perceives is reported.
options.feedback: Correct. Everything reported is what the child perceives and counts, so the narration stays with that viewpoint.

options.text: Second person, because the reader is asked to experience the scene directly.
options.feedback: Wrong. The reader is not addressed directly, so this is not second person.

options.text: An omniscient narrator, because the weather is described from outside.
options.feedback: Wrong. Nothing is reported that the child could not observe, so there is no external narration.

options.text: An objective narrator, because the child's thoughts are not described.
options.feedback: Wrong. The counting shows a specific mental activity, which rules out a purely objective report.

questions.explanation:
Point of view is determined by what the narration is able to report: only what one character perceives, or more than that character knows.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that uses a participle clause correctly.
questions.context: A student is writing a narrative about a misunderstanding.

options.text: Turning the corner, Marta was seeing her friend waiting at the bus stop.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was seeing' is not a passive form, so the clause is not grammatical here.

options.text: Turning the corner, Marta saw her friend waiting at the bus stop.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Turning the corner' is a participle phrase that modifies the subject and correctly shares its reference.

options.text: Turning, Marta saw her friend waiting at the bus stop.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Turning' without an object leaves the participle phrase incomplete.

options.text: Turning corner, Marta saw her friend waiting at the bus stop.
options.feedback: Wrong. The noun after 'turning' is required to complete the phrase.

questions.explanation:
A participle phrase must carry its own subject and object and must refer to the same person as the main clause.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that avoids informal wording.
questions.context: A student is writing a narrative in a formal register.

options.text: The meeting got called off, so the guys found out by email the next day.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Got called off', 'guys' and 'found out' are all informal in this register.

options.text: The meeting was off, so they let the applicants know by email the next day.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The meeting was off' is informal and 'let them know' is conversational.

options.text: The meeting had been cancelled, so the applicants were informed by email on the following day.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Cancelled', 'applicants' and 'informed' are all appropriate for a formal account of events.

options.text: The meeting was off, so the people were told the next day by email.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The meeting was off' is informal and the reordering obscures who was informed.

questions.explanation:
Formal narrative avoids contracted and conversational vocabulary while keeping the sequence of events clear.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which the adverbial correctly places an action in the past sequence.
questions.context: A student is building a narrative with a time signal.

options.text: Later three days the letter finally arrived, and nothing had changed.
options.feedback: Wrong. Moving 'later' after the numeral breaks the phrase, and the second clause must remain past simple.

options.text: Three days later the letter finally arrived, and nothing has changed.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Has changed' moves the final clause to the present and is inconsistent with the past narrative.

options.text: Later the letter finally arrived three days, and nothing has changed.
options.feedback: Wrong. Separating 'later' from 'three days' destroys the time phrase, and 'has changed' breaks the past frame.

options.text: Three days later the letter finally arrived, and nothing had changed.
options.feedback: Correct. The time phrase opens the main clause and the second clause stays in the past simple, which is consistent.

questions.explanation:
A past narrative keeps every clause in the past, so an adverbial is added without disturbing the tense of the surrounding clauses.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which revision fixes the inconsistency in the original sentence 'He arrived at the station, and he waited at the platform for an hour'?
questions.context: A student is revising a narrative to remove an inconsistency.

options.text: He arrived at the station and waited at the platform for an hour.
options.feedback: Correct. Removing 'he' before the second verb is the natural fix, since repeating the subject is unnecessary between coordinated clauses.

options.text: He had arrived at the station and he waits at the platform for an hour.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Had arrived' places the arrival even earlier than the waiting and 'waits' is present.

options.text: He arrives at the station, and he waited at the platform for an hour.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Arrives' in the present is inconsistent with 'waited' in the past.

options.text: He arrived at the station, and he is waiting at the platform for an hour.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is waiting' introduces a present continuous that contradicts a completed hour of waiting.

questions.explanation:
A repeated subject between two coordinated clauses in the same tense can normally be dropped, and tense consistency is the real requirement.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which opening places the reader in the scene immediately?
questions.context: A student is choosing how to open a story.

options.text: The following account describes an unusual journey that its writer later found memorable.
options.feedback: Wrong. The opening announces the account rather than placing the reader in it.

options.text: Water ran along the platform and gathered around her shoes before she had stepped off the bus.
options.feedback: Correct. The opening places the reader in a specific moment with concrete sensory detail and no framing.

options.text: There are many stations on that line and some of them are very old.
options.feedback: Wrong. The opening is a general comment about the line and involves no character or scene.

options.text: It was raining that day, which is something that often happens in that part of the country.
options.feedback: Wrong. The generalisation about the weather removes the reader from the particular moment.

questions.explanation:
An in medias res opening begins inside the action, whereas a framing opening distances the reader from the scene.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which statement best describes the effect of the flashback in a story?
questions.context: A student is analysing a narrative's structure.

options.text: It removes the need to narrate the present, since the earlier event covers everything.
options.feedback: Wrong. The present sequence still has to be narrated; the flashback does not replace it.

options.text: It proves that the present sequence could not have happened without the earlier event.
options.feedback: Wrong. A flashback may explain a reaction, but it does not prove that the present event was impossible.

options.text: It interrupts the present sequence to show an earlier event that explains the character's present reaction.
options.feedback: Correct. This describes the explanatory function of a flashback, which is to supply the cause of a present reaction.

options.text: It slows the story down without adding any information about the character.
options.feedback: Wrong. A well-placed flashback adds information about motive, which is what this structure is for.

questions.explanation:
A structural device is best evaluated by the information it contributes to the reader's understanding.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which justification best explains the use of one-word sentences at the height of a story's tension?
questions.context: A teacher asks a student to justify a narrative choice.

options.text: One-word sentences are required by the examiner for any narrative task.
options.feedback: Wrong. No examination rule requires any particular sentence length.

options.text: One-word sentences allow more detail to be included in the same paragraph.
options.feedback: Wrong. Short sentences use fewer words, so they leave less room for detail rather than more.

options.text: One-word sentences are always easier to read and are therefore the best default choice.
options.feedback: Wrong. Very short sentences are not easier to read, and there is no rule making them a default.

options.text: Short sentences slow the reader's eye down to a stop, which sharpens the pause the moment requires.
options.feedback: Correct. This ties the technique to the intended effect on the reader at that specific moment.

questions.explanation:
A justification of technique must connect the device to the intended effect rather than appeal to a general preference.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence best signals that a narrator is unreliable?
questions.context: A student is assessing an unreliable narrator in a narrative.

options.text: The market was the largest in the region, and everyone knows it, though the town had barely a hundred stalls.
options.feedback: Correct. The contradiction between the boast and the stated size, reinforced by the aside, marks the claim as untrustworthy.

options.text: The market was large, according to the town's own description of itself.
options.feedback: Wrong. Attributing the claim to the town distances the narrator from it, which is a reliable move.

options.text: The market was, without question, the finest in the whole of the south, which is the sort of claim that markets make about themselves.
options.feedback: Wrong. The narrator explicitly flags the boast as the kind of claim markets make, which undermines rather than supports it.

options.text: I counted the stalls myself: there were four, and I counted them twice.
options.feedback: Wrong. Counting the stalls twice is exactly what a reliable narrator would do.

questions.explanation:
An unreliable narrator is signalled by self-contradiction, unwarranted certainty or a clash between claim and evidence.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which statement best explains the difference between a summary and a retelling of a story?
questions.context: A student is comparing a summary with a retelling.

options.text: A retelling shortens the story, while a summary always tells it in full.
options.feedback: Wrong. It reverses the two: a retelling normally tells the whole story and a summary shortens it.

options.text: A retelling keeps the original sequence of events, while a summary may reorder them as long as the main outcome is preserved.
options.feedback: Correct. This distinguishes sequence preservation from the compression that allows reordering, which is the real difference.

options.text: A retelling includes dialogue, while a summary never may.
options.feedback: Wrong. Both forms may include dialogue, in different amounts.

options.text: A retelling changes the ending, while a summary must keep it unchanged.
options.feedback: Wrong. A retelling does not change the ending; it reports the ending it was given.

questions.explanation:
Distinguishing two forms of retelling depends on whether the original sequence is preserved or the content is compressed and reorganised.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which the interruption is correctly expressed.
questions.context: A student is writing a narrative and needs an interruption for realism.

options.text: She is halfway across the yard when a car called from the gate.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is halfway' presents the background in the present and is inconsistent with 'called'.

options.text: She was halfway across the yard when a car is calling from the gate.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is calling' shifts the interruption to the present and breaks the past frame.

options.text: She was halfway across the yard when a car called from the gate.
options.feedback: Correct. The past continuous background and the past simple interruption form the standard pattern.

options.text: She was halfway across the yard while a car has called from the gate.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Has called' is the present perfect, which cannot interrupt a past continuous clause in this way.

questions.explanation:
An interruption in a past narrative requires a past continuous background clause and a past simple interrupting clause.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses the tense correctly with 'since'?
questions.context: A student is checking a narrative for an inaccurate verb tense after a time expression.

options.text: She had worked at the depot since she arrived in the city.
options.feedback: Wrong. The past perfect needs a past reference point of its own, which 'since she arrived' does not supply.

options.text: She worked at the depot since she arrived in the city.
options.feedback: Wrong. The past simple would place the whole period in the past, and 'since' then reads incorrectly.

options.text: She is working at the depot since she arrived in the city.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Since' cannot be used with the present continuous in this way.

options.text: She has worked at the depot since she arrived in the city.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Since' with a past reference point takes the present perfect, which links the past start to the present.

questions.explanation: Since marks a period running from the past up to now, so the present perfect is the tense that matches it.
